dedupe_keys.name: data informed synthetic water distribution networks for resilience analysis in mayaguez puerto rico

description: This case study builds synthetic water distribution models for Mayagüez, Puerto Rico, from sparse public pipe data and tests how well they reproduce a detailed validation model for resilience analysis. Kirk Bonney, Katherine Klise and colleagues at Sandia National Laboratories, Oregon State University and Arizona State University published it in Water in November 2024. They assemble a validation model of 7,496 pipes, 6,287 junctions, 124 tanks, 89 pumps and 6 reservoirs from the Puerto Rico government GIS portal, then generate synthetic networks along OpenStreetMap roads using 0, 50 and 100 percent of the real pipe data with spatial association and a modified minimum cost flow method, and compare topology, diameters, pressures and response to a disruption in WNTR and EPANET. With half of the pipe data, average pressure error fell to 23.5 m of head from 31.6 m with none. Coverage is the Mayagüez service area. Format and access: an open access paper; the synthetic models are not released. Licence: CC-BY-4.0 for the article; free. Caveats: the models were not calibrated and results are for one city. It shows how sparse utility data can yield usable resilience testbeds. Related catalogue records are WNTR and the PipeNetGen synthetic network method.

outcomes: A validation model of 7,496 pipes, 6,287 junctions, 124 tanks, 89 pumps and 6 reservoirs was built from public data; a synthetic model using 50% of real pipe data matched its pressures with an average error of 23.5 m of head, against 31.6 m for a synthetic model using no pipe data.
